props.title: Triangle
props.initialSlug: A woman trapped in a deadly time loop at sea

sections.content: **Triangle** (2009) stands as one of the most ingeniously crafted time-loop thrillers, taking the cyclical narrative structure of **Groundhog Day** (1993) into dark psychological horror territory. Director Christopher Smith creates a nautical nightmare that shares DNA with **The Shining** (1980) and **Memento** (2000), using its repeating timeline to explore guilt, grief, and the desperate lengths someone will go to change fate. Like **Coherence** (2013), it takes a small-scale setting and transforms it into a mind-bending puzzle box.

sections.content: The genius of Triangle lies in how it builds its loops within loops, each cycle revealing new layers like **Primer** (2004) but with more emotional weight. The abandoned cruise ship setting echoes **Ghost Ship** (2002) and **Event Horizon** (1997), but Smith uses this isolation to amplify the psychological horror rather than rely on pure gore. Melissa George's performance as Jess carries the complex narrative through its spiraling iterations, each loop adding depth to her character's tragic motivations.

The film's influence can be seen in later temporal horror pieces like **The Endless** (2017) and **Time Trap** (2017). Its sophisticated handling of causality loops predates similar concepts in **Looper** (2012) and **Tenet** (2020), though Triangle maintains a tighter focus on personal horror over grand sci-fi concepts. The way it handles its revelations shares DNA with psychological thrillers like **Identity** (2003) and **Session 9** (2001). SUBHEAD: Psychological Horror and Maritime Setting

sections.content: Triangle's maritime setting isn't just atmospheric window dressing - it's integral to the film's themes of being lost and adrift, both literally and metaphorically. This puts it in conversation with other psychological horror films set at sea like **Below** (2002) and **Death Ship** (1980), while its time-bending narrative complexity rivals later films like **Source Code** (2011) and **Edge of Tomorrow** (2014). The ship becomes a character itself, like the Overlook Hotel in **The Shining** (1980), its endless corridors and identical passages amplifying the sense of being trapped in an eternal loop.
